tiers.essentials:
## Essentials

### What a speech is for

Every speech has one job: change what the audience thinks, feels, or does. Before you write a word, answer this: what do you want different by the end?

Three things decide your message. Not you alone.

1. **You** — your expertise, your goal.
2. **Your audience** — what they need, what they already know.
3. **Your occasion** — why this talk, why now.

Ignore any one of the three and the speech falls flat.

### Are all speeches the same? No.

A toast is not a sales pitch. A team update is not a conference keynote. Same skills, different shape. Check the occasion before you plan the content.

### Three Phases of Preparation

Every talk gets built in three phases, in this order. Learn the phases. Use them every time you prepare.

**1. Planning** — decide what you're going to say before you write a word of it.
1. **Purpose** — the change you want in your audience.
2. **Message** — the one thing you want them to remember after.
3. **Content** — the facts and examples that support your message.
4. **Structure** — the order you present that content in.
5. **Visual Aids** — what you'll show to support the message, not replace it.

**2. Writing** — turn the plan into actual words.
1. **Drafting** — write the script.
2. **Honing** — edit it. Cut anything that reads well but doesn't say well out loud.

**3. Practice** — turn the script into a spoken talk.
1. **Delivery** — voice, body, pace. How you actually say it.

Weak spot in any phase sinks the whole talk. Check all three, every time.

### Online changes part of Planning

Purpose and audience analysis shift online. A muted, half-watching audience on a screen is not the same room as people sitting in front of you.

- In person: you read faces, adjust live.
- Online: you can't. Assume shorter attention, more distraction. Plan for it before you start.

Ask "who is this for, in person or on a screen" every time. Never assume the same plan works both ways.

### Activity: Presentation history checklist

Five minutes. Grab a pen.

1. List every presentation you've given — work, school, anywhere. Three is enough if that's all you've got.
2. Next to each, write one thing that worked.
3. Next to each, write one thing that didn't.
4. Circle the pattern — the thing that shows up more than once.
5. Write one goal for this course, one sentence: "By the end, I want to ___."

Keep this page. You'll check it again later.
tiers.standard:
## Standard

### What a presentation is actually for

It's worth starting from a basic question, because skipping it is how presentations go wrong before a single slide gets made: what is this speech actually supposed to do? A presentation isn't primarily an act of information transfer — audiences can read a document for that — it's an attempt to change something in the listener: a belief, a decision, an emotional state, or a next action. Framing your task this way, before you touch structure or slides, changes what "good" looks like for the rest of your preparation.

That change is shaped by three factors working together, not by the speaker alone. The speaker brings expertise and a goal; the audience brings existing knowledge, expectations, and needs; and the occasion brings constraints — the reason this talk is happening now, in this format, for this length of time. A message that ignores any one of these three tends to miss, even if the content itself is accurate and well-organized, because "good content" is only good relative to who's receiving it and why.

### Are all speeches the same?

No, and treating them as if they were is a common early mistake. A toast, a project update, and a conference keynote all draw on the same underlying skill set, but they differ enormously in purpose, tone, and structure, so a plan built for one will often feel wrong in another. Before you prepare content, it's worth explicitly naming the type of speech you're giving and what "success" looks like for that specific occasion, rather than defaulting to a general-purpose template.

### Three Phases of Preparation

A useful way to organize how you get ready for a talk is to think of preparation as three sequential phases, each with its own components, rather than a flat list of things to check. Sequencing it this way solves a real problem: it's hard to know what to say before you know why you're saying it, and it's hard to know how you'll say it before you've actually written it down.

**Phase 1: Planning.** This is where you decide what the talk is actually going to be, before you draft a single sentence of it.

- **Purpose** is the specific change you want in your audience by the end — not a topic, but an outcome.
- **Message** is the one thing you want your audience to walk away remembering. It's the single sentence your entire talk is organized around, and it's worth getting precise about early, since everything else in Planning is built to support it. (Unit 2 covers how to test whether you actually have a real message, rather than just a restated topic.)
- **Content** is the material itself — the facts, examples, and evidence that support your message — filtered for what's true, relevant, and useful to this particular audience rather than everything you know.
- **Structure** is the order and shape that content takes, so the audience can follow the logic rather than just receive facts.
- **Visual Aids** are the slides, props, or other visual support you'll use, planned now because they shape what you'll actually be able to do later, during Delivery — you can't practice standing beside a screen you haven't designed yet.

**Phase 2: Writing.** This is where the plan becomes actual words on a page.

- **Drafting** is writing the script out in full, working from the plan rather than starting from a blank page.
- **Honing** is editing that draft specifically for the ear rather than the eye — cutting sentences that read fine on paper but sound stiff or overlong out loud, since spoken and written language behave differently.

**Phase 3: Practice.** This is where the written script becomes an actual spoken talk.

- **Delivery** covers voice, pacing, and body language — the physical and vocal execution of the talk, built on top of everything decided in the first two phases.

A talk can have a strong plan and still fail in Delivery, or have a clear purpose and still lose the room through weak Structure — the three-phase framework works as a checklist precisely because weakness at any stage can undercut everything that came before it.

### Purpose and audience analysis look different online

Two of these elements — Purpose and the audience analysis that feeds into Content and Structure, both part of Planning — need to be reconsidered specifically for online delivery, because an online audience is not simply an in-person audience viewed through a screen. In person, you can read faces and body language in real time and adjust your pacing or emphasis accordingly; online, that feedback loop is largely gone, and attention is competing with notifications, other browser tabs, and the general fatigue of screen-based meetings.

Practically, this means your purpose statement and your read of the audience need to build in shorter attention spans and more fragmented focus from the outset, rather than assuming the same plan will simply transfer. Ask explicitly, for every talk you prepare: is this being delivered in person or on a screen, and what does that change about what the audience can actually absorb?

### Activity: Presentation history inventory and goal-setting

Take about fifteen minutes for this exercise, either before your next session or at its start.

1. List the presentations you've given so far — professional, academic, or informal. Three or four is a reasonable starting point if your experience is limited.
2. For each one, note briefly what worked and what didn't. Be specific rather than general ("lost the room around the data slide" is more useful than "it was okay").
3. Look across your list for a pattern — a strength or a weakness that shows up more than once. That recurring item is often the most useful thing to work on this course.
4. Write a single personal goal for the course: one sentence describing what you want to be able to do differently by the end.
5. In pairs or small groups, share your pattern and your goal with a partner. Listening to someone else's inventory is often as useful as reflecting on your own, since it surfaces habits you might not have named in yourself yet.

Keep this inventory — later units will ask you to revisit it as your skills develop.
tiers.long:
## Long

### What is a presentation actually trying to do?

It's worth pausing on a question that's easy to skip past on the way to slide design: what is a presentation actually for? The honest answer is that it isn't primarily about transferring information — if that were the goal, a well-written email or report would usually do the job better, since it can be read at the recipient's own pace and referred back to. A presentation earns its place as a format when something needs to happen that a document can't easily do: build shared understanding in a room in real time, persuade people who might resist a cold written argument, or create a moment of shared attention and emotional weight around a decision. Thinking of your task this way — as an attempt to change something in your audience, whether that's a belief, a decision, or a next action — tends to produce a sharper, more useful talk than thinking of it as "covering the material."

That change doesn't happen in a vacuum; it's shaped jointly by three things, and it's worth treating all three as live variables rather than assuming your own expertise is the only ingredient that matters. You bring knowledge and a goal. Your audience brings its own prior knowledge, its expectations, and its needs, which may not match what you assume going in. And the occasion brings its own logic — why this talk is happening now, in this room or on this platform, in this amount of time, for this particular reason. A talk that's accurate and well-prepared can still miss badly if it ignores what the audience already knows, or misjudges what the occasion actually calls for. Worth asking yourself, before you prepare anything else: if I only got to choose one of "know my content," "know my audience," or "know my occasion" to get right, which would matter most for this specific talk? The answer isn't always the same, which is itself useful to notice.

### Are all speeches the same?

Clearly not, though it's tempting — especially early on — to reach for one general-purpose template and apply it everywhere. A wedding toast, a team status update, and a conference keynote share an underlying skill set: attention to audience, clarity of message, competent delivery. But they differ substantially in purpose, tone, expected length, and what "success" even looks like. A toast that succeeds by being warm and brief would fail badly as a keynote; a keynote that succeeds by being ambitious and wide-ranging would feel wildly out of place as a toast. Rather than asking "how do I give a good speech" as a single question, it's more useful to ask "what does a good version of this speech, in this context, actually look like" — and to let that answer, rather than a fixed template, drive your preparation.

### A framework for checking your work: three phases of preparation

One durable way of thinking about what makes a presentation succeed or fail is to break preparation into three phases, each containing a small number of components, rather than treating the whole thing as one undifferentiated task called "getting ready." This unit will use these terms throughout the course, so it's worth sitting with each one rather than skimming past the list — and it's worth understanding why the phases come in this order, not just memorizing them.

**Phase 1: Planning.** Before you write a word of an actual script, you're deciding what the talk is going to be. This phase has five components, and they build on each other:

- **Purpose** — the specific change you're aiming for in your audience by the end of the talk. Not "the topic," but the outcome: a decision made, a belief shifted, an action taken.
- **Message** — the single sentence you want your audience to walk away with. This is worth distinguishing carefully from Purpose: Purpose is the change you're aiming for in the audience's head; Message is the actual claim you'll make in order to produce that change. "I want the board to approve this budget" is a Purpose. "We should approve this budget because it pays for itself within a year" is a Message. Unit 2 goes into real depth on this distinction, including a simple test for whether you've actually written a message or just a restated topic — it's one of the more common places a talk quietly goes wrong before anyone's even started drafting slides.
- **Content** — the material itself: the facts, evidence, and examples that support your message, filtered for what's relevant and useful to this particular audience rather than everything you happen to know about the subject.
- **Structure** — the order and shape that content takes, so the audience can follow your reasoning rather than simply receive a list of facts. Structure has to come after Content for a practical reason: you can't meaningfully order material you haven't gathered yet, even if you already have a rough sense of your message before you've assembled the evidence for it.
- **Visual Aids** — slides, props, or other visual material, used to reinforce the message rather than replace or duplicate it. It's worth noticing that Visual Aids sits inside Planning, not off on its own at the end of the process. That's a deliberate placement: what you put on a screen shapes what you're able to do later, during Delivery — where you'll stand, when you'll pause, what you'll point at — so deciding your visual aids after you've already planned your delivery gets the dependency backward.

**Phase 2: Writing.** Once the plan exists, it has to become actual language, and that's a distinct enough task to deserve its own phase.

- **Drafting** — writing the script in full, working outward from the plan rather than starting from a blank page and hoping the plan surfaces on its own.
- **Honing** — a distinct editing pass, specifically for the ear rather than the eye. Spoken and written language behave differently — a sentence that reads cleanly on the page can sound stilted or overlong the moment it's spoken aloud — so this step exists to catch exactly that gap, deliberately separated from the act of drafting so you're not trying to write and edit in the same motion.

**Phase 3: Practice.** Only once a script exists does it make sense to rehearse saying it.

- **Delivery** — the physical and vocal execution: voice, pacing, body language, presence. Delivery comes last because it's the one component that depends on everything else already being settled; you can't meaningfully rehearse a talk whose content, structure, and slides are still in flux.

It's worth being honest that this ordering is a strong default, not an ironclad law — some experienced speakers work non-linearly, sketching a rough Structure early and letting it pull Content toward it, or drafting a rough script before their Message has fully crystallized, then using the draft itself to discover what they're actually trying to say. Treat the three-phase order as the reliable path on a first pass, and feel free to loop back a phase if something later in the process reveals a problem earlier in it — discovering during Honing that your Message doesn't quite hold up is a legitimate reason to return to Planning, not a sign you did something wrong.

Think about a presentation you sat through recently that didn't quite work. Try tracing it back through these phases — was the purpose actually clear, or was the speaker really just "covering the topic"? Was there a real message, or just a restated theme? Was the content right for that audience, or pitched for a different one? Often the weak point turns out to sit earlier in the process than it first appears — a delivery problem that's actually a planning problem wearing a delivery costume.

### Purpose and audience analysis change shape online

Two of these elements — Purpose, and the audience analysis that feeds directly into Content and Structure, both part of Planning — deserve specific reconsideration when a talk moves online, because it's a mistake to treat an online audience as simply an in-person audience that happens to be viewing through a screen. In a room, you have a continuous, if imperfect, feedback loop: you can see confused expressions, restless shifting, or genuine engagement, and adjust your pacing or emphasis accordingly, often without consciously deciding to. Online, most of that signal disappears — cameras may be off, reactions are delayed or absent, and you're competing directly with email, chat, and the general fatigue that comes from back-to-back video calls.

This doesn't mean the underlying purpose of a talk needs to change, but it does mean your assumptions about attention and retention should. It's reasonable to assume shorter sustained focus, more fragmented attention, and a real risk of losing people silently, with no visible cue that it's happening. Some presenters respond by building in more frequent structural signposting online, or shorter segments with more explicit checkpoints — not because the content is different, but because the audience's capacity to track a long unbroken argument is often lower in that setting. The practical habit worth building now, at the start of the course, is to ask explicitly for every talk you prepare: is this in person or on a screen, and what does that actually change about what this audience can take in? Different formats will call for different answers, and there's no single fixed adjustment that covers every case — it's a question to ask fresh each time, not a rule to apply mechanically.

### Activity: Presentation history inventory and goal-setting

Set aside fifteen to twenty minutes for this, ideally at the very start of the course, since the value of the exercise partly comes from having something concrete to look back on later.

1. Write down the presentations you've given so far, in any context — work, school, community, informal. If your experience is limited, three or four is a perfectly reasonable list; if you've given many, pick the ones that stand out for good or bad reasons.
2. For each one, reflect honestly on what worked and what didn't. Push past generic answers ("it went fine") toward something specific enough to be useful ("I lost people around the third slide because I'd stopped looking up from my notes").
3. Look across the whole list for a pattern rather than treating each talk as an isolated event. Is there a strength that keeps showing up? A weakness? Patterns across several talks are usually more diagnostic than any single talk's outcome, since a one-off stumble might just be circumstance, while a repeated one usually points at something worth deliberately working on.
4. Write one personal goal for the course — a single sentence describing what you want to be genuinely different about your presenting by the end. Try to make it specific enough that you'd know if you'd hit it, rather than something as broad as "be more confident."
5. Share your pattern and your goal with a partner or small group, and listen to theirs in return. This isn't just a social warm-up — hearing someone else narrate their presentation history often surfaces something useful about your own that you hadn't quite put into words, and starting the course by speaking out loud, even briefly, is itself a small first rep of the habit you're here to build.

Hold onto this inventory. Later units will ask you to return to it, both to track whether the pattern you identified is shifting and to check your goal against what you're actually practicing.

notes: REVISED 2026-07-07: the original 'flat 6 Keys' framework (Purpose, Content, Structure, Language, Delivery, Visual Aids as six equal, non-sequential checklist items) was replaced at the user's direction with a '3 Phases of Preparation' framework: Planning (Purpose -> Message -> Content -> Structure -> Visual Aids), Writing (Drafting -> Honing), Practice (Delivery). Reasons for the change, in case a future editor wonders why this differs from Decision 7 in the plan: (a) 'Language' as a label was too vague/generic and was actually describing a narrow editing task (checking a drafted script reads well aloud) -- renamed 'Honing' and moved into a new Writing phase alongside 'Drafting'; (b) Visual Aids was originally listed last, implying it's decided after Delivery, which is backwards -- slides have to be planned before Delivery because they constrain what Delivery can do (where you stand, when you pause); it now sits inside Planning, right after Structure; (c) 'Message' did not previously exist as a named element of this framework at all, despite Unit 2 building an entire Theme-vs-Message distinction on top of it -- Message is now formally introduced here (as 'the one sentence you want the audience to remember'), explicitly distinguished from Purpose (the audience-side outcome) and from Content (the supporting material), with Unit 2 flagged as the deep-dive unit for testing whether a candidate message is real. Cross-tier consistency locks for the assembly pass: (1) The 3 phases and their 8 named sub-elements (Purpose, Message, Content, Structure, Visual Aids, Drafting, Honing, Delivery) must be named identically and in this exact order across all three tiers and any future unit that references 'the framework from Unit 1' -- do NOT reintroduce 'the 6 Keys' or 'Language' anywhere else in the manuscript. (2) The 'three factors' (speaker/you, audience, occasion) that shape a message are a separate, earlier concept in this same unit (answering 'who decides the message') and should not be confused with the 8-element Phases framework -- both exist in this unit but are distinct. (3) The online vs. in-person distinction is scoped to Purpose + audience analysis, both part of Planning. (4) The self-assessment/goal-setting activity produces a 'presentation history inventory' with a stated personal goal this unit says will be revisited in 'later units' -- whichever unit covers rehearsal, feedback, or a capstone/final presentation should plan a callback to this inventory and goal. (5) Standard and Long tiers both add a peer share-out step to the activity that Essentials omits. (6) DOWNSTREAM CHECK NEEDED: search the rest of the manuscript (especially Unit 2, which already has its own Theme-vs-Message content) for any references to 'the 6 Keys' or 'Language' as a named key, and update to match this revised framework.
